title: Why can a small tumor have large effects?
lead: A tumor the size of a grape can turn skin yellow, change blood sugar and cause back pain. The reason is where it sits, not how big it is.

steps.title: A crowded neighborhood
steps.text: The pancreas lies across the back of the upper abdomen, and its head is tucked into the curve of the duodenum. Through that head runs the lower bile duct; behind its neck pass the superior mesenteric and portal veins; the superior mesenteric artery lies just behind the uncinate process; and the nerves of the celiac plexus and the first lymph node stations surround all of it. In about one person in six the right hepatic artery takes an unusual route through this same space [[ANAT-007]]. A tumor here does not need to be large to touch something that matters.

steps.title: Blocking the bile duct
steps.text: Bile made by the liver must pass through the pancreatic head to reach the intestine. A head tumor of modest size can pinch that duct shut, so bilirubin spills into the blood: skin and eyes yellow, urine darkens, stools turn pale and the skin itches. Among all the symptoms recorded before a diagnosis, jaundice is the one that most specifically points to pancreatic cancer [[ANAT-010]]. It is also why head tumors tend to be found earlier than tumors in the body or tail, which have no duct to block and are more often already spread when found [[ANAT-003]].

steps.title: Blocking the pancreatic duct
steps.text: The main pancreatic duct carries digestive enzymes from the acinar cells to the duodenum. A tumor across the duct dams it, so the duct upstream dilates and the gland behind it stops delivering enzymes, even though those cells are still healthy. Enzyme insufficiency is already present in roughly two-thirds of people at diagnosis [[ANAT-021]], producing bloating, greasy stools and weight loss. In mice, losing enzyme delivery by itself was enough to drive early loss of body fat [[ANAT-027]], which is one reason weight can fall before anyone suspects a tumor.

steps.title: Changing blood sugar from a distance
steps.text: The islets that make insulin are spread through the whole gland, so a small tumor cannot destroy enough of them to cause diabetes. Yet fasting glucose begins drifting upward roughly two to three years before diagnosis [[ANAT-016]], and diabetes is present in about 40 to 47 percent of patients, three-quarters of it new, independent of tumor size or location [[ANAT-015]]. This is a paraneoplastic effect: the tumor releases signals that impair insulin action and secretion, and in more than half of patients the diabetes improves after the tumor is removed [[ANAT-015]]. A metabolic change can therefore be the earliest sign of a physically tiny cancer.

steps.title: Reaching the nerves
steps.text: Pancreatic cancer grows along nerves. Perineural invasion is found in about 80 percent of resected tumors, mostly in the nerves outside the gland, and it is associated with positive margins, nodal spread and shorter survival [[ANAT-013]]. The pain this produces is felt in the upper abdomen and often the back, because the celiac plexus that the tumor reaches carries sensation from the whole upper abdomen. The intensity of pain tracks inflammatory cells gathered around nerves more than the depth of invasion [[ANAT-002]], and early lesions can even suppress pain for a time [[ANAT-012]], which is why back pain is so often attributed to something else.

steps.title: Touching the vessels
steps.text: The same geometry decides whether a tumor can be removed. The neck of the pancreas crosses the superior mesenteric vein, and the uncinate process reaches toward the artery. A tumor that wraps more than halfway around the vein has a roughly 70 to 80 percent chance of truly invading its wall and nearly always requires a vein resection, yet margins were clear just as often across contact grades once a vein resection was planned [[DIAG-001]]. Contact with the artery is treated more cautiously because arteries cannot be rebuilt as safely. Size matters less than millimeters of contact.

steps.title: What this means for you
steps.text: Location explains why symptoms can be dramatic while the tumor is small, why some tumors are found early and others late, and why two tumors of the same size can lead to different plans. It also explains why relieving an obstruction, replacing enzymes or treating blood sugar can make someone feel markedly better without changing the cancer itself. When you read your own imaging report, the words to look for are which part of the pancreas, which duct is dilated, and which vessels are touched.

title: How does a pancreatic cell become a cancer cell?
lead: A normal cell grows only when told to, stops when damaged, and dies when it should. Cancer is what remains when those rules are broken, one at a time or several at once.

steps.title: A cell that waits for permission
steps.text: Acinar and duct cells in the pancreas divide rarely. When a growth signal arrives at a receptor on the surface, it switches on the protein KRAS, which passes the message inward through the MAPK and PI3K pathways to the nucleus, and then switches itself off within minutes. Separate brakes watch the cell cycle: CDKN2A's p16 holds the cell before it copies its DNA, p53 halts a cell with damaged DNA and can order its death, and TGF-β signals through SMAD4 to tell epithelial cells to stop dividing. Each of these is lost or hijacked in most pancreatic cancers.

steps.title: A switch stuck on
steps.text: Almost every pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma carries a KRAS mutation, around 90 percent in sequenced cohorts, most often the G12D version [[GENE-002]]. The mutation does not create a new signal; it stops KRAS from switching off, so the cell behaves as if growth factors were always present. In mice, established tumors collapse within about a week when mutant KRAS is turned off, but most later relapse and about half of those relapses no longer need KRAS at all [[GENE-012]][[GENE-013]]. KRAS is the engine, but it is not the whole machine.

steps.title: The lesion that is almost always harmless
steps.text: KRAS mutations are the earliest change in the microscopic precursor lesions called PanINs, present in over 90 percent of even the lowest-grade ones [[ORIG-002]]. Those lesions are astonishingly common: three-dimensional mapping finds hundreds in an ordinary adult pancreas [[ORIG-001]]. Since the lifetime risk of pancreatic cancer is under 2 percent, the overwhelming majority of mutant cells never progress. In adult mice a KRAS mutation in acinar cells is held in check by a state called oncogene-induced senescence, and episodes of pancreatitis release that brake [[ORIG-014]]. A single stuck switch is necessary but far from sufficient.

steps.title: Which cell, and by which route
steps.text: In mice, classic mucinous PanIN arises mainly from acinar cells that reprogram into a duct-like state, a process that requires the transcription factor Sox9 [[ORIG-012]]. Duct cells can also give rise to cancer, but by a route that largely skips low-grade PanIN and reaches invasion faster [[ORIG-003]]. There is no single staircase. Some lesions found beside a cancer were induced in genetically normal neighbors rather than being its ancestors [[ORIG-003]], and cystic precursors such as IPMN follow their own genetics and their own, mostly slow, natural history.

steps.title: Losing the brakes, sometimes all at once
steps.text: Progression from low- to high-grade PanIN is marked less by new point mutations than by loss of the chromosome regions carrying CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 [[ORIG-023]]. Whole-genome sequencing shows that this is often not gradual: 65 percent of tumors showed chromosome shattering (chromothripsis), 45 percent had doubled their entire genome, and in 16 percent several of the canonical brakes were knocked out by a single catastrophic event [[GENE-003]]. The textbook sequence of one mutation after another describes some tumors; a sudden rearrangement describes many others.

steps.title: What the losses allow
steps.text: Each lost brake adds a capability. Without p16, the cell copies damaged DNA. Mutant p53 does more than remove a safety check; in mouse models it actively drives invasion and metastasis, and removing it from tumor cells reverses that behavior [[GENE-020]]. SMAD4 is lost in roughly a third of tumors, and an autopsy series linked its loss to death from widespread metastasis rather than local growth, although a study of resected tumors found no such association, so the link is not settled [[GENE-023]]. These changes also shape treatment: CDKN2A status itself does not predict response to drugs aimed at the cell cycle, whereas retained RB protein does [[GENE-009]].

steps.title: A cancer cell is a state, not a fixed identity
steps.text: Even after the genome is set, the same cell can behave differently. Pancreatic cancer cells move along an axis from a classical state to a basal-like one, and basal-like tumors do worse [[GENE-004]]. Organoids shift toward the basal state when exposed to TGF-β, mutant-p53 cells switch under stress and switch back, and single cells can express both programs at once [[GENE-014]][[GENE-015]]. Metastases can arise without any new driver mutation, through reprogramming of chromatin marks rather than DNA sequence [[GENE-008]]. That plasticity is part of why resistance appears without a mutation to explain it.

title: What surrounds the cancer cells, and why does it matter?
lead: Most of a pancreatic tumor is not cancer. It is scar-like tissue, fibroblasts, immune cells, collapsed vessels and starved space, and each part changes what treatment can do.

steps.title: A tumor that is mostly scar
steps.text: Pancreatic cancer provokes a dense, fibrous reaction around itself, a process called desmoplasia. Fibroblasts and stellate cells activate, lay down collagen and hyaluronan, and the tumor becomes hard and pale. On a contrast CT scan this is why the tumor enhances less than normal pancreas: there is less blood in it. Microvessel density in human pancreatic cancer is four to five times lower than in normal pancreas, even though the same tissue secretes growth factors that should make vessels sprout [[TME-009]]. The scar is not inert packaging; it is the environment the cancer cells live in.

steps.title: Pressure and perfusion
steps.text: In mouse tumors, hyaluronan binds water and generates interstitial pressures of about 75 to 130 mmHg against 8 to 13 in normal pancreas, enough to collapse most vessels [[TME-003]]. Only about a third of the vessels present carried blood, and the active form of gemcitabine was undetectable inside the tumor [[TME-001]]. Removing hyaluronan with an enzyme reopened vessels and raised drug delivery more than sixfold [[TME-003]]. The mechanism is real and was measured directly. The question was whether fixing it would help people.

steps.title: The experiment that reversed the story
steps.text: When investigators deleted the hedgehog signal that drives stroma, or chronically blocked it with a drug, or ablated myofibroblasts outright, mouse tumors became more aggressive, more vascular, more metastatic, and the animals died sooner [[TME-002]][[TME-012]]. The stroma had been restraining the cancer as well as shielding it. The immune system carried the effect: myofibroblast loss expanded regulatory T cells, and blocking CTLA-4 reversed the acceleration [[TME-012]]. 'Break down the scar tissue' turned out to be an unsafe description of a treatment goal.

steps.title: What happened in patients
steps.text: The hyaluronidase that worked in mice went into a biomarker-selected phase 3 trial of 492 patients. Tumors shrank more often with the drug, 47 versus 36 percent, but overall survival was 11.2 versus 11.5 months, a hazard ratio of exactly 1.00 [[TME-004]]. A drug that blocks autophagy told the same story twice: more responses on scans, no improvement in survival, and no proof its target was even engaged in the tumor [[TME-027]][[TME-026]]. These trials are the best lesson in the atlas: a tumor that shrinks on a scan is not the same as a person who lives longer.

steps.title: Fibroblasts are not one thing
steps.text: The contradiction resolved when fibroblasts turned out to be several populations. Cells pressed against the cancer glands become myofibroblasts under direct contact and TGF-β; cells farther away become inflammatory fibroblasts under tumor-secreted interleukin-1; a third state carries antigen-presenting machinery [[TME-005]][[TME-011]][[TME-017]]. In matched transplants, one fibroblast lineage suppressed tumor growth while another permitted it, and the suppression vanished in mice without adaptive immunity [[TME-036]]. Depleting a single pro-tumor subtype slowed growth and improved checkpoint response, the opposite of bulk removal [[TME-037]]. The goal shifted from demolition to reprogramming.

steps.title: Immune cells present but kept away
steps.text: Killer T cells are usually in the tumor, and how close they get to cancer cells, within about 20 micrometers, tracks with longer survival [[TME-010]]. Collagen does not wall them off; chemical signals do. Stellate cells coat the cancer cells with CXCL12 and hold T cells in the stroma, and blocking that receptor in mice brought T cells in and uncovered activity of checkpoint antibodies that did nothing alone [[TME-018]][[TME-019]]. In patients, checkpoint drugs alone produce almost no responses: 0 and 3.1 percent in a randomized phase 2 [[TME-007]]. The barrier is positional and functional, not structural.

steps.title: Starved, scavenging, and still growing
steps.text: Human pancreatic tumors measured against the patient's own adjacent pancreas were depleted of both glucose and glutamine [[TME-028]]. Cancer cells with mutant RAS respond by drinking in extracellular fluid and digesting its proteins for amino acids, and by relying on autophagy, the recycling of their own components, even without treatment [[TME-008]][[TME-025]]. Stellate cells feed them alanine [[TME-029]]. Every one of these is a plausible drug target, and the autophagy inhibitor already tested in patients failed to help. Understanding the ecosystem is necessary; it is not the same as being able to change it.

title: Why give chemotherapy before or after surgery?
lead: Surgery removes what can be seen. Chemotherapy is aimed at what cannot. The order depends on what the evidence says about each situation.

steps.title: Two kinds of disease
steps.text: A scan shows disease above a few millimeters in size. Below that, the only way to know cells are present is to wait and see whether they grow. Genetic reconstruction of autopsy cases suggests the clone that will form metastases arises within the primary years before the cancer becomes lethal [[SURG-002]], and growth modeling implies most patients already carry microscopic deposits at diagnosis [[SURG-009]]. In mice, cells leave the pancreas and reach the liver before a tumor is even visible under the microscope [[SURG-001]]. Every plan for localized disease is really a plan for both kinds of disease at once.

steps.title: Why surgery alone is rarely enough
steps.text: A margin-negative operation removes the visible tumor, not the disease. About half of recurrences after resection appear within the first year [[SURG-007]], and roughly one in five up-front operations for anatomically resectable tumors is followed by death or recurrence within six months [[SURG-008]]. This is why systemic therapy is part of nearly every curative-intent plan. The question is whether it comes after the operation, before it, or both.

steps.title: After surgery: the adjuvant evidence
steps.text: The strongest evidence is for chemotherapy after surgery. In patients under 80 who recovered well and had a CA 19-9 below 180, six months of modified FOLFIRINOX gave a median survival of 53.5 months versus 35.5 with gemcitabine, and five-year survival of 43 versus 31 percent [[TX-003]]. The cost was toxicity: 55 percent stopped oxaliplatin early, and neuropathy keeps worsening for about three months after the last dose [[TX-003]][[TX-022]]. The catch is that these were the fittest patients; many never recover enough to start, and in a perioperative trial only 78 to 79 percent of resected patients began their planned postoperative treatment [[TX-013]].

steps.title: Before surgery: what it guarantees
steps.text: Giving chemotherapy first ensures that systemic treatment happens, treats microscopic disease during the months when surgery and recovery would otherwise leave it alone, and acts as a test: a tumor that spreads during chemotherapy would have spread after surgery, and that person is spared an operation that would not have helped. In a prospective borderline-resectable trial, 5 percent progressed during eight cycles and were spared surgery while 65 percent of everyone enrolled reached a margin-negative resection [[TX-012]]. It also makes clear margins more likely: preoperative chemoradiation raised the margin-negative rate from 40 to 72 percent [[TX-004]].

steps.title: The same strategy, different answers
steps.text: For borderline resectable tumors, treatment first improved five-year survival in a randomized trial [[TX-004]]. For tumors that are clearly resectable on imaging, randomized trials of chemotherapy first have not shown a survival benefit, and one suggested harm [[TX-L11]][[TX-013]]. One explanation is that the benefit has two parts, converting a likely positive margin into a clear one and delivering early systemic therapy to people who would otherwise never get it, and both parts are smaller when the baseline margin risk is low and adjuvant completion is likely [[INF-TX-01]]. Trials comparing perioperative with adjuvant treatment in resectable disease are still running.

steps.title: Reading the numbers you will be shown
steps.text: Survival figures quoted for people who reached surgery after neoadjuvant therapy describe a selected group: 2-year survival of 72 percent among the resected versus 56 percent among everyone who started treatment, in one trial [[TX-011]]. Response on the scan during chemotherapy is also an imperfect guide: treated scar looks like tumor, so about 70 percent of resected tumors still looked locally advanced or borderline on imaging yet 92 percent came out with clear margins [[DIAG-004]]. Ask which group a number describes and when its clock started.

steps.title: What the plan is really trying to do
steps.text: Every sequence is a bet about microscopic disease: treat it early and test the tumor's behavior before a major operation, or operate first and treat afterward if recovery allows. Neither is a universal rule, which is why plans differ between centers and change after restaging. The useful questions for a care team are which category the tumor is in, what the restaging will measure, and what would make the plan change.

title: What makes a tumor removable?
lead: Stage, vessel contact, resectability and fitness are four different questions. A plan depends on all of them, and a scan answers only some.

steps.title: Stage is about extent
steps.text: Stage describes how far the cancer has reached: the size of the tumor, whether lymph nodes contain cancer, and whether it has spread to distant organs. In the current system, the number of involved nodes separates survival strongly, with five-year survival of about 36, 21 and 11 percent for zero, one to three, and four or more nodes, while tumor size separates it only weakly once nodes are accounted for [[DIAG-003]][[DIAG-017]]. Stage is assigned twice: clinically from scans before treatment, and pathologically from the specimen afterward, and the two often differ.

steps.title: Resectability is about geometry
steps.text: Resectability asks a different question: can a surgeon remove the tumor with a clear margin without destroying something the body needs? The categories are potentially resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced and metastatic. 'Borderline' is a statement about anatomy, a tumor on the border between removable and not, and has nothing to do with 'borderline malignant'. Two tumors of identical stage can sit in different categories because one touches a vessel and the other does not.

steps.title: Veins can be rebuilt
steps.text: The superior mesenteric and portal veins run directly behind the neck of the pancreas, so many tumors touch them. On a pancreas-protocol CT the degree of contact predicts whether the vein wall is truly invaded: contact of more than half the circumference carried a 70 to 80 percent chance of invasion and nearly always required vein resection, yet margin-negative rates did not differ by contact grade once a vein resection was planned [[DIAG-001]]. Resecting and reconstructing the vein gives outcomes comparable to cases that did not need it [[SURG-017]], and invasion of the vein wall predicts outcome better than the measured margin distance [[SURG-006]].

steps.title: Arteries are different
steps.text: Arteries carry the blood supply to the intestine and liver, and rebuilding them is far riskier than rebuilding a vein. Contact with the superior mesenteric artery or celiac axis of more than half the circumference, or any involvement that cannot be reconstructed, usually places a tumor in the locally advanced category, and arterial involvement is what defines T4 in the staging system regardless of size. Chemotherapy before surgery is used in part to test whether such a tumor can be brought to an operation; in large series about one in five locally advanced tumors is eventually resected [[SURG-019]].

steps.title: After treatment, the scan lags
steps.text: Chemotherapy and radiation leave scar where tumor was, and scar has the same density as tumor on CT. In a series treated with FOLFIRINOX, about 70 percent of tumors still looked locally advanced or borderline on restaging yet 92 percent were removed with clear margins [[DIAG-004]]. Metabolic activity on PET fell by about 65 percent while size fell by only 10 percent [[DIAG-008]]. Pathologists themselves agree only moderately on how much tumor a treatment killed [[DIAG-010]]. Many surgeons therefore decide at operation, not from the restaging scan alone.

steps.title: Fitness is the fourth question
steps.text: A Whipple operation carries operative mortality of a few percent even in expert hands and far more at low-volume hospitals [[SURG-003]], and a pancreatic fistula occurred in 30 percent of the highest-risk glands in a nationwide series [[SURG-016]]. Recovery takes months and can delay or prevent adjuvant chemotherapy. Whether someone can tolerate the operation and its aftermath depends on heart, lungs, nutrition, muscle and support at home, none of which appear on a CT. Fitness, not stage, is sometimes the deciding factor.

steps.title: What hidden disease means for the decision
steps.text: Even after CT, MRI and PET, about one patient in six thought to have localized disease is found to have hidden spread at staging laparoscopy [[DIAG-002]]. This is why 'resectable on the scan' is a provisional label, why a plan can change at operation, and why removing the primary is not the same as removing the disease. Resectability answers whether an operation is possible; the other three questions decide whether it is wise.

title: What does a clear scan tell us?
lead: A clear scan is good news with limits. Imaging, blood markers and microscopic disease are three different measurements, and none of them sees everything.

steps.title: What a scan can see
steps.text: CT and MRI detect masses above a few millimeters and changes in how tissue takes up contrast or restricts the diffusion of water. Below that threshold a deposit is invisible, and even above it a small liver spot is often indeterminate: cysts, hemangiomas and treated scar all occur, which is why follow-up imaging rather than a single scan settles most of them. About half of first recurrences after surgery appear in the liver [[SURG-015]], so the liver is where the question matters most.

steps.title: Treated tissue looks like tumor
steps.text: After chemotherapy, a mass that persists on CT may be scar, live tumor or a mixture, and the three cannot be separated by density. In resected specimens, tumors that still looked unresectable on imaging came out with clear margins 92 percent of the time [[DIAG-004]]. The reverse also holds: a tumor that is 'not well visualized' may have shrunk, or may be hidden by scar and motion artifact. Diffusion-weighted MRI and PET add information, but PET's metabolic signal can fall far more than size does [[DIAG-008]], and comparing to the right prior scan matters as much as the scan itself.

steps.title: CA 19-9: useful when it works
steps.text: CA 19-9 is a sugar molecule shed into blood, and its trend during treatment tracks survival [[DIAG-014]]. It has two blind spots. Between 5 and 12 percent of people are Lewis-negative and cannot make it at all, so a normal value means nothing for them [[DIAG-014]][[DIAG-015]]. And bile-duct blockage inflates it: in benign obstruction the level fell by about 76 percent after drainage [[DIAG-016]]. For non-secretors, CEA or CA-125 may substitute, and imaging carries the load. For everyone else, the direction of the trend after bilirubin normalizes is more informative than any single number.

steps.title: Looking for DNA instead
steps.text: Dying tumor cells shed fragments of DNA into blood, and a test can look for the tumor's mutations there. After surgery, detectable tumor DNA marks people who almost always recur and flags recurrence about three months before a scan does [[DIAG-007]][[DIAG-012]]. The test is less helpful before treatment of small tumors, where fewer than half shed enough to detect [[DIAG-011]]. It is a strong positive signal and a weak negative one.

steps.title: Why a negative test is not proof
steps.text: Detection depends on how much DNA the tumor sheds and on the few tumor copies a blood tube can hold, so small deposits sit below the floor. About half of patients with a negative post-operative test still recur [[DIAG-012]][[DIAG-024]]. Handling the tumor at surgery can itself raise the measured signal transiently [[DIAG-025]], and plasma can report mutations from aging blood cells rather than the cancer [[DIAG-026]]. No ctDNA test is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer decisions as of October 2026. A negative result means none detected, not none present.

steps.title: What a clear scan does mean
steps.text: A clear scan after treatment means no deposit large enough to see, which is the best result imaging can report and is associated with longer survival. It does not mean no cancer cells, which is why adjuvant therapy is given to people with clear scans and why follow-up continues for years. Dormant cells in the liver can remain immune-invisible for long periods before awakening [[SURG-012]], which is the mechanistic reason late recurrences happen, not a prediction that they will.

steps.title: Holding both truths
steps.text: The honest position is neither false reassurance nor fatalism. Each clear scan narrows the range of what could be present and lengthens the time in which nothing has grown, and that time has real value. Each measurement has a floor, and the floor is why surveillance is scheduled rather than declared finished. The useful questions are what interval the care team recommends, which markers apply to you, and what finding would change the plan.

title: When can a molecular result change the options?
lead: Four different kinds of result come back from testing, and they answer four different questions: inherited risk, tumor targets, treatment toxicity and trial eligibility.

steps.title: Four results, four questions
steps.text: A molecular workup can report inherited (germline) variants carried in every cell of the body, acquired alterations found only in the tumor, state or expression markers such as the classical or basal-like program, and variants in drug-metabolism genes that predict toxicity. Each matters to a different person: germline findings to relatives as well as the patient, tumor findings to drug choice, state markers mostly to research, and toxicity variants to dosing safety. Keeping them apart avoids the most common confusions.

steps.title: Inherited findings
steps.text: About 5.5 percent of people with pancreatic cancer carry an inherited mutation in a predisposition gene, most often ATM, BRCA2, CDKN2A, BRCA1, TP53 or MLH1, and most of them have no family history [[ORIG-006]]. That is why testing is offered to everyone with the diagnosis rather than only to those with affected relatives. A positive result can open a treatment option for the patient and surveillance for relatives; imaging surveillance of high-risk relatives finds more cancers at an early stage, although how much of that is lead time is still debated [[ORIG-004]].

steps.title: When BRCA changes treatment, and when ATM does not
steps.text: Cells lacking BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 cannot repair double-strand breaks well, which makes platinum drugs and PARP inhibitors more effective against them. The benefit concentrates in tumors where both copies of a core gene are lost [[GENE-016]]. The label is not enough: in a trial that enrolled by gene name across BRCA, PALB2, ATM and CHEK2, median progression-free survival on a PARP inhibitor was only 2 months, yet every durable responder with evaluable data had lost both copies [[GENE-025]]. Maintenance olaparib for germline BRCA carriers doubles progression-free survival without a proven survival gain [[TX-005]]. ATM is not BRCA.

steps.title: The rare targets in the tumor
steps.text: Most targetable findings cluster in the 10 to 13 percent of tumors without a KRAS mutation, where gene fusions appear in about one in five [[GENE-005]]. Mismatch-repair deficiency, which makes a tumor responsive to pembrolizumab, is found in under 1 percent [[GENE-006]], and the response in that rare group was 4 of 22 in the pivotal cohort rather than the 'about half' seen across other cancers [[TX-007]]. These are real options for a few people and irrelevant to most, and a tissue test can miss them, which is why the test chosen matters.

steps.title: The target almost everyone has
steps.text: KRAS, mutated in about 90 percent of tumors, became a drug target in practice in 2026. In a randomized phase 3 of 500 previously treated patients, the RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib roughly doubled median survival, 13.2 versus 6.7 months, with a hazard ratio of 0.40, and the US FDA approved it on 26 August 2026 for metastatic disease after at least one prior therapy [[RAS-033]]. The label requires no mutation test, though the trial's endpoints were defined in RAS G12-mutant patients. Whether it helps after surgery, when no disease is visible, is being tested for the first time in the adjuvant RASolute 304 trial, which has no results yet.

steps.title: Variants that change dosing, not the tumor
steps.text: Two inherited variants predict toxicity rather than response. People with low-activity UGT1A1 clear irinotecan's active metabolite poorly, and a 30 percent starting-dose reduction brought their severe toxicity down to everyone else's level without worse survival [[GENE-018]]. DPYD variants impair breakdown of fluorouracil and can cause severe early toxicity; genotype-guided dosing reduced serious toxicity in a prospective program [[GENE-019]]. The US capecitabine label now directs DPYD testing before treatment while noting that no FDA-authorized test exists, and the irinotecan label advises considering UGT1A1 testing. These results protect the patient, not the tumor.

steps.title: Yield is not benefit
steps.text: When advanced tumors are sequenced prospectively, about 48 percent carry something someone would call therapeutically relevant [[GENE-022]]. In a registry of 1,856 referred patients, only 58 percent ever received a report, 26 percent had an actionable finding, and 2 percent received a matched therapy; the widely quoted survival advantage for matched treatment comes from a comparison within that 2 percent [[GENE-029]]. Testing is worth doing because the rare findings are decisive for the people who have them. It is not a promise that an option will appear.

title: Why can digestion and energy change after treatment?
lead: The pancreas makes the enzymes that digest food and the insulin that stores it. Tumor, surgery and chemotherapy each change that, and each change has a response.

steps.title: The gland that digests and stores
steps.text: The exocrine pancreas secretes about two and a half liters a day of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice: acinar cells release enzymes that break down fat, protein and starch, and duct cells add bicarbonate so those enzymes work once food leaves the acid of the stomach [[ANAT-009]]. The islets scattered through the gland release insulin and glucagon to store and release fuel. A tumor, an operation or an inflamed gland can disrupt either system, and the symptoms are the same whether the cells are gone or simply cannot deliver.

steps.title: When enzymes stop arriving
steps.text: A tumor that blocks the duct, or an operation that removes part of the gland and rebuilds the plumbing, means food reaches the intestine without enough enzyme. Fat passes undigested, so stools become greasy, pale and hard to flush, the abdomen bloats, weight falls and fat-soluble vitamins run low. Roughly two-thirds of people already have enzyme insufficiency at diagnosis [[ANAT-021]]. In the United States most patients are never tested for it and only about one in twenty receives an adequately dosed prescription [[SUPP-001]].

steps.title: Replacing what is missing
steps.text: Enzyme capsules taken with meals supply the lipase, protease and amylase the gland no longer delivers. In a placebo-controlled trial after pancreatic surgery, high-dose enteric-coated enzymes raised fat absorption by about 25 percentage points [[SUPP-002]]. After a Whipple only about a quarter of patients regain near-normal absorption even on high doses, because the rebuilt anatomy mixes enzymes and food imperfectly [[SUPP-002]], so persistent symptoms are a reason to revisit timing, dose and acid suppression with the care team rather than to assume nothing more can be done. Enzymes relieve symptoms within weeks; claims that they lengthen survival come from non-randomized comparisons [[SUPP-020]].

steps.title: Blood sugar before and after
steps.text: Diabetes in pancreatic cancer has two different causes. Before treatment it is usually paraneoplastic, caused by signals from the tumor, present in 40 to 47 percent of patients and improving in more than half after resection [[ANAT-015]]. After surgery it reflects lost islet mass and the metabolic state of what remains: new diabetes develops in roughly a quarter to a third within one to three years of a partial pancreatectomy, most often in people with obesity, a borderline HbA1c or a fatty remnant [[SUPP-004]][[SUPP-035]], and in everyone after a total pancreatectomy [[SUPP-036]]. Knowing which kind you have changes what to expect.

steps.title: Why weight and muscle fall
steps.text: Weight loss has more than one engine. Maldigestion removes calories, nausea and taste changes reduce intake, and the tumor itself drives cachexia, a wasting of muscle and fat signaled by cytokines such as GDF-15. During chemotherapy, loss of skeletal muscle predicts shorter survival even when weight is stable [[SUPP-003]]. Blocking GDF-15 with an antibody raised body weight by up to 2.8 kilograms over twelve weeks in a placebo-controlled phase 2 trial that included pancreatic cancer, the first direct evidence that a cytokine drives the process in people [[SUPP-014]]; a phase 3 is recruiting and nothing of this kind is yet approved.

steps.title: What helps, and what the evidence shows
steps.text: Simple interventions have measurable effects. In a blinded trial after surgery, 18 grams a day of extra protein raised intake and improved walking speed and quality of life [[SUPP-016]], whereas six months of resistance training alone did not change CT-measured muscle [[SUPP-015]]. Exercise during preoperative treatment improved walking capacity, and resected tumors from exercisers showed more vessels and more killer T cells, an experimental finding rather than a proven benefit [[SUPP-017]][[SUPP-018]][[SUPP-019]]. None of this is a verdict on effort; it is a map of where effort has been shown to pay.

steps.title: Energy, mood and the long view
steps.text: Fatigue after treatment has many sources: anemia, deconditioning, cytokines, poor sleep, pain and the drugs themselves. Five or more years after a Whipple, overall quality of life sits in the normal range, although pancreatic-type pain and bowel symptoms persist for many [[SUPP-031]]. Depression lowers the chance of being offered surgery or chemotherapy and explains much of its associated survival gap [[SUPP-009]], so mood is a medical issue, not a private one. Digestion, blood sugar, muscle and mood each have a specialist, and asking for them is part of treatment.
